headline: Vietnam Creates Major Reserve to Save World's Rarest Monkey
meta_description: Vietnam establishes a 3,182-hectare conservation reserve in Ninh Binh Province to protect Delacour's langur, one of Earth's most endangered primates with fewer…
summary_short: Vietnam is taking decisive action to save Delacour's langur, an extremely rare primate with fewer than 250 individuals remaining. A new conservation reserve spans limest…
body:
Vietnam has established the Kim Bang Delacour's Langur Habitat Conservation Area, a sweeping effort to protect one of the world's most critically endangered primates. Spanning 3,182 hectares across three wards in Ninh Binh Province—Ly Thuong Kiet, Tam Chuc, and Nguyen Uy—the reserve encompasses pristine karst limestone forests and mountain scenery to provide a dedicated sanctuary for Delacour's langur. Named after the French biologist who first identified the species, this monkey now clings to survival with perhaps just 17 populations totaling somewhere between 200 and 250 individuals worldwide. While several national parks already exist across northern Vietnam where these animals live, the parks do not always overlap with the langur's actual habitat, leaving critical gaps that the new reserve now addresses.

The reserve divides its protection strategy into two zones. Approximately 4,400 acres will remain strictly guarded for the species' direct protection, while another 3,500 acres have been earmarked specifically for ecological restoration. These efforts matter because Delacour's langur reproduces slowly—females mature around age four, bear single infants after seven-month gestations, and nurse their young for 21 months. The reserve's management plans will monitor population trends carefully, accounting for these natural constraints on recovery.

Beyond safeguarding the langur itself, the project aims to strengthen forest quality across the region through enhanced protection and restoration measures. Authorities are also weaving community engagement into the initiative, planning to raise public awareness and gradually develop ecotourism that ties economic opportunity to biodiversity conservation. For a species hovering at the edge of extinction, this multifaceted approach offers genuine hope—turning a corner of northern Vietnam into a working model of how human communities can reverse course and save what remains of our natural world.
quick_facts: Fewer than 250 Delacour's langurs remain in 17 populations worldwide
3,182-hectare reserve spans three wards in Ninh Binh Province, Vietnam
Named after French biologist who first identified the species
Females carry single infants for 7 months and nurse for 21 months
4,400 acres designated for strict protection; 3,500 for restoration
